And we said that this amounts to finding a path from V0, the source vertex to VK, the

So, we argued that we could easily do this for small graphs visually, but if we want
to write an algorithm, we need a way of representing the graph. So, the first thing we decided
was that we would name the vertices 1 to n. So, if we have n vertices, we will just

an adjacency matrix. In this adjacency matrix, the ijth entry indicates the presence or absence
of an edge from vertex i to vertex j. So, a ij is 1, if there is an edge, a ij is 0, if
there is no such edge. In this matrix, if we want to find out where the pair of vertices
are directly connected, we just have to probe the appropriate entry. So, we can do that
in constant time to find all the outgoing neighbors of a vertex, we have to scan the
row for that vertex. So, that takes linear time in terms of the number of vertices.
Now, one thing we observed is that typically in many graphs, this matrix is largely 0.
Most pairs are not connected. So, we can get a more compact representation by just listing
out the neighbors of each vertex. So, instead of keeping a row of 1s and 0s, we just record
those vertices whose entries are 1. So, this gives us a more efficient representation

exploring the graph systematically. Each time we went to a vertex, we would mark it as
visited and then we had to make sure that when we were exploring vertices, we did not
re-explore the same vertex twice. So, we said there would be two fundamental strategies,
breadth first and depth first. So, today we are going to look at breadth first search.
So, the idea of breadth first search is to explore the graph level by level. So, we start
at the source vertex and we now explore all the vertices which are one step away connected
by a direct edge to the source vertex. Then we look at all vertices which are newly connected,
one step away from level one vertices. So, these are two steps away from the source
vertex. Then for three steps and so on. Now, while we are doing this exploration, we
have to keep track of two quantities. We have to first note of course, whether a given
vertex has been visited, has it been explored, is it connected to the source vertex? Also,
for each such vertex, we have to explore its neighbors. So, for each vertex, we need to
know a, has it been visited and we may not be able to explore it as soon as it is visited.
So, we need to remember that we have explored it or not explored it and those which are
not explored, we have to make sure we explore them once. So, the way to do this is to use
some data structures to keep track of these quantities. As we said, the set of vertices
is numbered one to n. So, we can keep an array visited with entries one to n which tells
us whether or not vertex i has been visited. Now, whenever we visit a vertex, we need to
subsequently explore it. Since we may not explore it immediately, we may have to keep it
pending for a while. So, we have to keep a collection of these vertices which have been
visited but have not yet been explored. There are many ways to do this, but one natural
way is to explore them in the order in which they were visited. So, if we want to explore
in the order in which they were visited, a natural data structure to keep the list of
unexplored but visited vertices is a queue. So, we put each visited vertex into the queue,
the first time we have come to it and then we process all the vertices in the queue until
all vertices have been explored. So, here are some high level pseudo-code for breadth
first search. When we reach a vertex i which we have visited for the first time, we will

explored later. So, we begin by marking the source vertex and adding it to the queue.
